output.methodChoice: Combination of A and D: the key issue is separating rival explanations that are perfectly overlapping in the data.
output.brief: Resignations are concentrated on one matter, not spread across the group. Eight of the 11 associates on Kestrel have left, against 1 of 13 who never worked on it. Other groups are normal, and the firm-wide hours target applies to everyone, so neither the target nor general market mobility explains this. Pay is a weak explanation, because the 12 non-Kestrel associates on the same pay mostly stayed. One caveat: all Kestrel associates report to Dorian Faulk, and he supervises nothing else. That means heavy workload on Kestrel and his supervision are completely tangled in the records. The survey points to both: months of weekend work and late-night public corrections. I can't separate them from the data we have, so I am not confident about which is the main driver. I have used 1 of my 2 evidence items. Don't pay the £12k retention payment and close the review. It targets the weakest explanation and would leave the Kestrel problem in place. Next steps: commission the £9k confidential external interviews, designed to separate supervision from workload. Add matter and supervising-partner fields to attrition tracking. Prepare a supervision change or contract reviewers, ready to act on what the interviews find. The Kestrel review phase runs to December 2026, so there's little time to waste.
